verses.1:1: And the word of the Lord came to Jonah, son of Amittai, saying,
verses.1:2: "Rise, and go to Nineveh, the large city, and preach in it, because its wickedness has gone up before Me."
verses.1:3: And Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord, and he went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish, and paid its fare, and went down into it to go with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.
verses.1:4: But the Lord sent a great wind onto the sea, and a great storm arose on the sea, and the ship was in danger of being shattered.
verses.1:5: And the sailors were afraid, and the men cried out to their own god, and they threw the goods that were in the ship into the sea so that it might be lightened of them; and Jonah went down to the interior of the ship and was sleeping in a heavy sleep.
verses.1:6: And the helmsman approached him and said to him, "Why are you weighed down with sleep? Rise, call upon your God, if perhaps God may think of us, and we may not perish."
verses.1:7: And each man said to his companion, "Come, and let us cast lots, and let us know why this evil is upon us." And they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.
verses.1:8: And they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil is upon us: what is your work? What is your land, and where are you going? Or from what people are you?"
verses.1:9: And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."
verses.1:10: And the men feared with a great fear and said to him, "Why have you done this?" For the men had learned that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.
verses.1:11: And they said to him, "What shall we do to you so that the sea will grow calm for us?" For the sea kept going on and swelling up.
verses.1:12: And he said to them, "Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will grow calm for you; for I know that because of me this huge storm has come upon you."
verses.1:13: And the men were rowing to return to the dry land, and they could not, because the sea kept going on and swelling up over them.
verses.1:14: And they cried out to the Lord and said, "We implore You, Lord, let us not perish for the life of this man, and do not lay innocent blood upon us; because You, Lord, have done as You willed."
verses.1:15: And they picked up Jonah and threw him into the sea, and the sea stood still from its raging.
verses.1:16: And the men feared the Lord with a great fear, and they offered sacrifices to the Lord and made vows.
verses.2:1: And the Lord prepared a large fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights.
verses.2:2: And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly of the fish,
verses.2:3: and said, "I cried out from my tribulation to the Lord, and He heard me; from the belly of the underworld I cried out, and You heard my voice.
verses.2:4: And You cast me into the deep, in the heart of the sea, and the current surrounded me; all Your whirlpools and Your waves passed over me.
verses.2:5: And I said, 'I have been cast away from the sight of Your eyes; nevertheless I will see Your holy temple again.'
verses.2:6: The waters surrounded me even to my soul; the abyss enclosed me, the open sea covered my head.
verses.2:7: I went down to the farthest ends of the mountains; the bars of the earth shut me in forever; and You will raise up my life from corruption, Lord my God.
verses.2:8: When my soul was in anguish within me, I remembered the Lord, so that my prayer may come to You, to Your holy temple.
verses.2:9: Those who observe vanities to no avail abandon their own mercy.
verses.2:10: But I, with a voice of praise, will offer sacrifice to You; whatever I have vowed, I will pay to the Lord for salvation."
verses.2:11: And the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry land.
verses.3:1: And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying,
verses.3:2: "Rise, and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it the preaching that I speak to you."
verses.3:3: And Jonah rose and went to Nineveh according to the word of the Lord; and Nineveh was a great city, a journey of three days.
verses.3:4: And Jonah began to enter the city, a journey of one day, and he cried out and said, "Forty days more, and Nineveh will be overthrown."
verses.3:5: And the men of Nineveh believed in God, and they proclaimed a fast and were clothed in sackcloth, from the greatest even to the least.
verses.3:6: And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne, and cast off his garment from himself, and put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
verses.3:7: And he cried out and spoke in Nineveh from the mouth of the king and his princes, saying, "Let people and beasts and cattle and flocks not taste anything; let them not graze, and let them not drink water.
verses.3:8: And let people and beasts be covered with sackcloth, and let them cry out to the Lord with might; and let each man turn from his evil way and from the iniquity that is in their hands.
verses.3:9: Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn back from the fury of His anger, and we will not perish?"
verses.3:10: And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way; and God had mercy concerning the evil that He had spoken of doing to them, and He did not do it.
verses.4:1: And Jonah was afflicted with great affliction, and he became angry.
verses.4:2: And he prayed to the Lord and said, "I implore You, Lord, was this not my word when I was still in my land? For this reason I acted beforehand to flee to Tarshish; for I know that You are a gracious and merciful God, patient and of great compassion, and forgiving concerning evil.
verses.4:3: And now, Lord, please take my soul from me, because death is better for me than life."
verses.4:4: And the Lord said, "Do you think you are rightly angry?"
verses.4:5: And Jonah went out from the city and sat down opposite the east side of the city; and he made a shelter for himself there, and was sitting beneath it in the shade until he might see what would happen to the city.
verses.4:6: And the Lord God prepared ivy, and it came up over Jonah's head, so that it might be shade over his head and protect him (for he had suffered); and Jonah rejoiced over the ivy with great joy.
verses.4:7: And God prepared a worm at the rising of dawn on the next day, and it struck the ivy, and it withered.
verses.4:8: And when the sun had risen, the Lord commanded a hot and scorching wind; and the sun struck on Jonah's head, and he was sweltering; and he asked for his soul that he might die, and said, "It is better for me to die than to live."
verses.4:9: And the Lord said to Jonah, "Do you think you are rightly angry over the ivy?" And he said, "I am rightly angry, even to death."
verses.4:10: And the Lord said, "You grieve over the ivy on which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which was born in one night and perished in one night;
verses.4:11: and should I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know what is between their right hand and their left, and many animals?"

notes.1:2: The Vulgate reads "preach in it" (prædica in ea) and singular "its wickedness" (malitia ejus), whereas the Hebrew text reads "cry out against it" and plural "their wickedness."
notes.1:8: The Vulgate asks "and where are you going?" (et quo vadis?), whereas the Hebrew text asks "where do you come from?"
notes.1:11: Latin "ibat, et intumescebat" (literally "kept going on and swelling up," repeated in 1:13) reflects a Semitic idiom for a storm growing steadily fiercer, while depicting the sea specifically as swelling up.
notes.2:1: As in the Hebrew, the Vulgate begins chapter 2 here, and it reads "prepared" (præparavit) where the Hebrew reads "appointed."
notes.2:3: Latin inferi ("the underworld," literally "the lower regions") renders Hebrew Sheol, the abode of the dead.
notes.2:6: The Vulgate reads "the open sea covered my head" (pelagus operuit caput meum), interpreting the Hebrew term for reeds or seaweed as the sea itself.
notes.2:7: Unlike the Hebrew past tense ("You brought up my life from the pit"), the Vulgate uses the future tense "You will raise up" (sublevabis) and reads "from corruption" (de corruptione), agreeing with the Septuagint.
notes.2:10: The Vulgate joins "salvation" to the preceding verb as "I will pay to the Lord for salvation" (reddam pro salute Domino), whereas the Hebrew closes with a separate exclamation, "Salvation belongs to the Lord."
notes.3:3: The Vulgate reads simply "a great city" (civitas magna); the Hebrew adds "to God," an idiom for "exceedingly great."
notes.3:7: The Vulgate reads literally "from the mouth of the king and his princes" (ex ore regis et principum ejus), whereas the Hebrew reads "by the decree of the king and his nobles."
notes.3:8: The Vulgate reads "cry out to the Lord" (ad Dominum) and "from the iniquity" (ab iniquitate), where the Hebrew reads "to God" and "from the violence."
notes.3:10: The Vulgate reads "God had mercy concerning the evil" (misertus est Deus super malitiam), where the Hebrew uses the verb for relenting and a term encompassing disaster or harm.
notes.4:2: Vulgate scio ("I know," present tense), patiens ("patient"), and ignoscens super malitia ("forgiving concerning evil") are distinctive Latin renderings where the Hebrew reads "I knew," "slow to anger," and "relenting concerning calamity."
notes.4:6: Vulgate hederam ("ivy") is Jerome's famous distinctive rendering of Hebrew qiqayon (often taken as a castor-oil plant; Septuagint "gourd"). The parenthetical (laboraverat enim) (lit. "for he had labored/suffered") renders Hebrew "to deliver him from his discomfort" as a brief causal note on Jonah's distress.
notes.4:8: Vulgate praecepit Dominus vento calido et urenti ("the Lord commanded a hot and scorching wind") has "the Lord" for Hebrew "God," uses "commanded" rather than "appointed," and omits "east"; aestuabat ("was sweltering") stands where the Hebrew has "grew faint."
notes.4:10: Vulgate distinguishes doles ("you grieve") here from parcam ("spare") in 4:11, whereas the Hebrew uses the same verb ("have pity/spare") in both verses; sub una nocte nata est ("was born in one night") reflects the Hebrew idiom "son of a night."
